clue.text: Interest by politician in Murdoch venture is most revealing

indicators.note: in places the interest and the politician inside the name of the Murdoch business

parts.note: Sky, the satellite broadcaster, was Rupert Murdoch's venture
I is the standard abbreviation for interest, as in banking formulas
an MP, Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A satirical jab: a politician's financial interest in a Murdoch business is the most revealing thing about them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most' here means 'very', as in 'most kind': the answer is a plain adjective, not a superlative.
explanation.definitionFit: Skimpy clothing covers little, so it shows a great deal of the body.

clue.text: Tiger den country?

parts.note: the Tamil Tigers were a separatist rebel group based on this island nation, so it was their den

explanation.walkthrough: Not a tiger reserve: the Tamil Tigers (LTTE) fought a civil war for a separate state in the north of this island.
explanation.definitionFit: The island nation south of India was home to the Tamil Tiger insurgency, making it the guerrillas' lair.

clue.text: Where camp types are found, by the sound of it, being highly strung

indicators.note: by the sound of it means the phrase heard aloud gives the answer, not its spelling

parts.note: campers are found in tents

explanation.surface: Flamboyant camp people are described as nervy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'camp types' suggests flamboyant people, but it means campers, who are found IN TENTS; 'by the sound of it' says that phrase heard aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A highly strung person is nervous and emotional, which is what an intense person is.

clue.text: Rag man reportedly looks over male member

indicators.note: over places the name above the rest in this down clue
reportedly says the word is as heard, so peers stands for a name that sounds the same

parts.note: to peer is to look closely
an organ is a member, a part of the body

explanation.surface: A rag-and-bone man is said to eye a man's private parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly' turns the looking word into the first name PIERS, which in this down clue sits 'over' the male member. He edited the Daily Mirror; a tabloid is a rag.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabloid newspaper is a rag, and the editor of the Mirror ran one, so he is a rag man.

clue.text: Jacobite, for instance, getting an erection

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745 were revolts against the crown
second meaning, read literally: a rising up, something going up

explanation.surface: A smutty Private Eye joke about a supporter of the Stuarts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Jacobites backed the exiled Stuart kings and rose in arms against the Hanoverian monarchy.
explanation.definitionFit: A revolt is a rebellion against authority, and the Jacobite rebellions are the textbook British example.

clue.text: Mock bonk goes on a good time

indicators.note: goes on means the good time is placed after it, carrying on from it in this down clue

parts.note: bonk and poke are both British slang for sex
fun is a good time

explanation.surface: Faked sex is a bit of a laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mock' looks like an adjective describing the bonk, but it is the verb, to ridicule; 'goes on' puts the good time after the slang for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: To ridicule someone is to make jokes at their expense, the idiom with 'at'.

clue.text: Somewhat undesirable organisation

indicators.note: Somewhat means only part of the next word is taken, so the letters sit inside it

parts.note: the letters run across the middle of undesirable

explanation.surface: A rather unsavoury group or body.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish Republican Army was a paramilitary body, so it is an example of a group.

clue.text: Really stupid nit with religious book

indicators.note: stupid suggests the word nit is muddled into a new order

parts.note: Ruth is a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: An idiot clutching a holy book is very foolish indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Really' looks like an intensifier for 'stupid', but it is the definition, and 'stupid' rearranges NIT into INT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbs used to say something is actually so, in fact or genuinely.

clue.text: Tasteless tabloid on the up gets one shut up

indicators.note: on the up means the word reads upwards in this down clue, so backwards

parts.note: a rag is a disreputable newspaper
I is the Roman numeral one
SH is the command for silence

explanation.surface: A vulgar tabloid on the rise is told to be quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Garish means showy and vulgar, which is what tasteless decor or clothing is.

clue.text: Sam's bust providing a huge erection

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters of Sam's are rearranged

parts.note: if means providing, on condition that

explanation.surface: Sam's bosom is said to produce an impressive arousal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' plays on the bosom, but it means broken. The erection is a mountain mass, not a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A massif is a compact group of mountains, something raised up on an enormous scale.

clue.text: Fashionable article on rugby player, as seen in the Eye

parts.note: something fashionable is 'in'
THE is the definite article
a back is one of the rugby positions behind the scrum

explanation.surface: A trendy item about a rugby player, as featured in Private Eye.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye is a British satirical magazine; its investigative news section is headed 'In the Back'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a regular section of Private Eye magazine, so it is something seen in that publication.

clue.text: Some editorial (Tara's) on which blood is spilled?

indicators.note: Some means only part of the following words is taken, so the letters lie inside them

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of editorial and the start of Tara's

explanation.surface: A bloodthirsty newspaper editorial written by someone called Tara.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes letters running across 'editorial (Tara's'. The question mark flags a definition by example: sacrificial blood was shed on an altar.
explanation.definitionFit: Animal sacrifices were made on a sacred table, so blood was spilled upon it.

clue.text: Places you used to visit, topless, for relations

indicators.note: topless means the first letter, the top of the word, is removed

parts.note: old haunts are places you once frequented

explanation.surface: Revisiting old haunts, perhaps in a topless state, to see the family.
explanation.definitionFit: Your parents' sisters are family members, so they are relations.

clue.text: Swampy, note, has carpets of grass and the like

parts.note: swampy ground is soft underfoot
D is one of the musical notes
rugs are small carpets

explanation.surface: Swampy, the 1990s road protester, owns carpets made of grass.
explanation.walkthrough: Swampy was a famous British eco-protester of the 1990s, which makes 'grass' look like turf; it is slang for cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: Grass is slang for cannabis, the classic example of a drug considered less harmful than heroin or cocaine.

clue.text: Underhand — has something that will shift the sod Murdoch!

parts.note: dirty means underhand, unfair

parts.words: something that will shift the sod
parts.note: a digger moves earth; sod is turf

explanation.surface: An abuse-laden attack calling Murdoch an underhand sod who deserves shifting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sod' looks like an insult for Murdoch but is turf. Private Eye calls Rupert Murdoch 'the Dirty Digger'; digger is also slang for an Australian.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Private Eye's long-running nickname for the Australian-born media tycoon Rupert.

clue.text: Look flipping ill — don't touch me!

indicators.note: flipping turns the word for a look over, so it reads backwards

parts.note: a peek is a quick look
off, as in 'feeling off', means unwell

explanation.surface: Someone who looks really ill warns others away from them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' poses as a mild British curse but turns PEEK into KEEP.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a command telling someone to stay away and not lay hands on you.

clue.text: Ollie's way

parts.note: Ollie is the nickname of the US marine at the heart of the Iran-Contra affair, and his surname is also a compass point

explanation.walkthrough: Lieutenant Colonel Oliver 'Ollie' North was the US marine at the centre of the 1980s Iran-Contra scandal; his surname doubles as a direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A compass point is a direction of travel, so it is a way to go, and it is also the surname of Ollie the marine.

clue.text: Union calls for head to get out of amorous carrying-on

indicators.note: head to get out of means the first letter leaves the word for the affair

parts.note: dalliance is flirtation or a casual love affair

explanation.surface: A trade union demands that its leader quit an affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' suggests a trade union, but it means any joining together. 'head to get out of' removes the D from DALLIANCE; 'calls for' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: An alliance is a joining of parties for a common purpose, which is a union.

clue.text: Flutter and shake next to Brenda

indicators.note: next to places the Queen's letters straight after the shake

parts.note: to wag is to shake, as a dog does its tail
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER (Elizabeth Regina)

explanation.surface: A trembling courtier shakes beside the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls Queen Elizabeth II 'Brenda', and her royal cipher goes 'next to' the shake. 'Flutter and shake' looks like one pair of synonyms, but only 'Flutter' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A flutter is British slang for a small bet, so the two words are synonyms for a gamble.

clue.text: Shakes as a result of unexpected BSE blow

indicators.note: unexpected suggests these letters land in an unforeseen order

explanation.surface: Farmers tremble after the surprise mad-cow disease setback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpected' rearranges BSE and BLOW together. BSE, mad cow disease, devastated British beef farming in the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are verbs for moving unsteadily from side to side, trembling.

clue.text: Falling down after sport, one has gumption

indicators.note: after places the rest after the sport

parts.note: RU is the abbreviation for Rugby Union
I is the Roman numeral one
nous is British slang for common sense

explanation.surface: A sportsman who keeps falling over is still a shrewd type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falling down' means dilapidated, as a building is, not toppling over; 'after' puts one and gumption behind the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruinous building is decaying and dilapidated, so it is collapsing.

clue.text: Easily-cracked nuts might make you divine

parts.note: crystal is fragile glass that cracks easily
nuts and balls are both slang for testicles

explanation.surface: A schoolboy joke about a delicate part of the anatomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divine' is the verb here, to foretell, not the adjective meaning heavenly.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortune-teller gazes into glass spheres to foresee the future, so these let you divine what is coming.

clue.text: Is able to walk arse over tip after cold drink

indicators.note: after places the overturned phrase after the cold letter

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

indicators.note: arse over tip is British slang for head over heels, so the phrase is turned backwards

parts.note: can means is able
to go is to walk

explanation.surface: Someone who can still walk tumbles over after a cold drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arse over tip', British slang for head over heels, turns 'is able to walk' backwards into OGNAC, which comes 'after' the cold letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cognac is a French brandy, so it is a kind of alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Sumatra's dispossessed distressed states

indicators.note: dispossessed drops the possessive ending and shakes the island's name out of its order

parts.note: the island's name, losing its possessive 's

explanation.surface: Displaced people on Sumatra are in a desperate condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dispossessed' does double duty: it strips the possessive 's from Sumatra's and signals that SUMATRA be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A trauma is a state of deep emotional shock, so the plural names states of distress.

clue.text: OK for a consumer journalist spewing bile

parts.note: ED is short for editor, a journalist

indicators.note: spewing suggests the letters of bile come out in a mess

explanation.surface: A consumer-affairs reporter rants furiously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'OK for a consumer' reads like product approval, but the consumer is someone eating. 'spewing' jumbles the bile into IBLE, after the journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Something edible is fit to be eaten, so it is fine for someone to consume.

clue.text: Hack's back, doing a Lord Lucan and exposing a lie

indicators.note: back means the word for the hack is read backwards

parts.note: a hack is a journalist, here taken as ED, an editor
Lord Lucan vanished in 1974 after his children's nanny was murdered; to do a bunk is to run off

explanation.surface: A journalist hits back, disappearing like Lord Lucan while unmasking a falsehood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses ED into DE. Lord Lucan, a British peer, disappeared in 1974 and was never found; 'doing a bunk' is British slang for running away.
explanation.definitionFit: To debunk a claim is to show that it is false, so the participle describes unmasking a falsehood.

clue.text: A national air display attended by Queen and Cyclops

indicators.note: attended by means the Queen and Cyclops follow the rearranged air
display suggests the letters of air are laid out afresh in a new order

parts.note: Q is the abbreviation for Queen, as in chess
Cyclops is the setter's name, and the setter is I; a cyclops also has one eye

explanation.surface: A national air show attended by the Queen and the crossword setter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'display' joins 'air display' in the surface but rearranges AIR into IRA, which is 'attended by' Q and I. Cyclops refers to himself as I.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Iraq is a citizen of that country, so one is a national of it.

clue.text: See 20
Just look at granny's former occupation!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: just to see or look
second meaning: Melita Norwood, the 'granny ...', was unmasked in 1999 as a former Soviet agent

explanation.walkthrough: In 1999 an 87-year-old British great-grandmother, Melita Norwood, was revealed to have passed secrets to the KGB for decades.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for catching sight of something and a noun for a secret agent.

clue.text: He's in order making love to sweep chappie

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, written O
a range is a sweep or extent
a chappie is a man

explanation.surface: A man, apparently orderly, making love to a chimney sweep.
explanation.walkthrough: The Orange Order is a Protestant fraternal organisation in Northern Ireland; its members are called Orangemen.
explanation.definitionFit: An Orangeman is a member of the Orange Order, the Protestant society in Ulster.

clue.text: Lamb sales poor: having lost 50 yen, it's hopeless

indicators.note: poor suggests the word sales is in bad shape and rearranged
hopeless says the letters gathered are in a muddle, to be reordered
having lost means the letter for fifty is removed from sales

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
Y is the currency abbreviation for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: A gloomy farm report: lamb prices so weak the market is hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb is Charles Lamb, who wrote as Elia. 'having lost' 50 takes L from SALES, leaving SAES; with Y and ITS, 'poor' and 'hopeless' rearrange the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lamb is famous for his Essays of Elia, so he is an example of a writer of short prose pieces.

clue.text: Terrible curse surrounds old Robinson

indicators.note: surrounds means the rearranged curse goes around the letter for old
terrible suggests the word curse is wrecked and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A dreadful curse hangs over an aged man called Robinson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' rearranges CURSE into CRUSE, which 'surrounds' O.
explanation.definitionFit: Robinson is the first name of Defoe's castaway hero, so the surname completes the famous name.
